terms.gloss: it (of a thing; of a fact or an idea)
terms.grammar: pronoun: neuter of is; genitive ejus, dative eī
evidence: Cic. Fam. 9.24.3: cūrā ut valeās; id forīs cēnitandō facillimē cōnsequēre
Cic. Sen. 21: crēdō, nisi eam exerceās
terms.comment: The neuter is for what has no gender in Latin: a fact, a clause, a deed (id forīs cēnitandō facillimē cōnsequēre). A noun keeps its own gender, so “it” is eam for memoria and eum for hortus. Very often Latin says nothing for “it”: as subject the verb carries it, and an object that is plain from the context is left out (Plaut. Aul. 641, ostendī, I’ve shown them).

terms.gloss: it (in “it is raining”, “it is getting dark”)
terms.grammar: construction: the verb alone in the third person singular
evidence: Quint. 6.3.66: nōn pluit, nōn opus est tibi
terms.comment: Weather, time and feeling verbs have no subject at all: pluit, it is raining; advesperāscit, it is getting dark; mē paenitet, I am sorry. Never id pluit.

evidence: Plin. Ep. 1.11.1: at hoc ipsum scrībe
terms.comment: Pointing at the thing present or the point just made: Quid est hoc? What is it?

phrases.latin: nōn pluit, nōn opus est tibi; sī pluit, ipse ūtar
phrases.english: If it isn’t raining, you don’t need it; if it is raining, I’ll wear it myself.

phrases.latin: Dīc mihi, aufūgistīne? — Era, factum. — Satin' id tibi placet? — Nōn. … Ūnam hanc noxiam mitte: sī aliam admīserō umquam, occīditō.
phrases.english: Tell me, did you run away? — Yes, madam. — Are you pleased with it? — No. … Let me off this one fault: if I ever do another, kill me.

phrases.latin: at memoria minuitur. crēdō, nisi eam exerceās
phrases.english: But memory fades. — I suppose it does, if you don’t exercise it.

phrases.latin: corium dēpressum in fluviō vīdērunt canēs. id ut comēsse extractum possent facilius, aquam coepēre ēbibere: sed ruptī prius periēre quam quod petierant contingerent
phrases.english: Some dogs saw a hide sunk in a river. To get it out and eat it more easily, they began to drink up the water; but they burst and died before they reached what they were after.

phrases.latin: cūrā ut valeās; id forīs cēnitandō facillimē cōnsequēre
phrases.english: Look after your health; you’ll manage it most easily by dining out a lot.

hic.against: Lewis & Short hīc, haec, hōc, marking the heavy syllable as a long vowel
hic.html: De Vaan 284, s.v. hic: the nominative is *hi-ke, so the vowel is short and the syllable heavy (hicc, p. 102, s.v. -ce); the adverb hīc, here, is the old locative *hoi-ke. Likewise the neuter hoc (hocc), against the ablative hōc.

sources: Lewis & Short: is · Lewis & Short: hic
Michiel de Vaan, Etymological Dictionary of Latin and the other Italic Languages (2008), pp. 102, 284.
